PAPER
An Approach for Hardware Trojan Detection using Triple Modular
Redundancy in Approximate Synthesis (HT-TRAPS)
Manal FATIMA†, Sa’ed ABED††, and Osman HASAN†, Nonmembers
SUMMARY
Approximate computing (AC) has been increasingly used to meet the
growing demand for energy-efficient and high-performance computing in
error-tolerant applications, particularly in the fields of machine learning,
signal processing, and multimedia applications.
Approximate synthesis
tools are an essential component in approximate circuit design and opti-
mization as they enable designers to trade-off accuracy for reduced power
consumption, area, and delay. However, these approximate synthesis tools
are quite vulnerable to adversarial attacks as it is quite challenging to dis-
tinguish between a change in the functionality of the given circuit due to
an approximation or a Hardware Trojan (HT). In this paper, we propose an
approach for HT detection using Triple modular Redundancy in APproxi-
mate Synthesis (HT-TRAPS) tools. The approach also utilizes functional
and side channel power and timing analysis to distinguish approximations
from HTs and is applicable for either identifying a clean netlist or detecting
the presence of a HT at the gate-level post-approximate synthesis stage. We
implement the HT-TRAPS approach using a full stack of open-source and
commercial tools, including BLASYS, ABACUS, SCOAP and Xilinx Vi-
vado, and thoroughly evaluate its effectiveness by detecting various Trojan
benchmarks, such as B19-T100, B19-T200, and B19-500 Trojans, inserted
in several circuits, such as the approximated Absolute Difference calculator,
Butterfly filter, a classifier, x2, a 16-bit Multiplier and a 32-bit Adder.
key words:
Approximate Computing, Approximate Synthesis, Hardware
Trojan (HT), Side Channel Analysis, Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR)

Introduction
Approximate computing [1] is a recently introduced
paradigm that allows optimization of power, speed, or area
by compromising the accuracy of digital arithmetic circuits.
The main idea is to reduce the computational overhead and
energy consumption of a system by relaxing the need for pre-
cise calculations. The use of approximate computing has be-
come increasingly popular in recent years due to the growing
demand for energy-efficient and high-performance comput-
ing systems, particularly in the fields of machine learning,
signal processing, and multimedia applications, which are
inherently error-resilient due to the perpetual limit of human
observers or the involvement of noise. However, the effec-
tiveness of approximate computing depends on the specific
application and the level of accuracy required.
Approximate computing can be applied at various levels
of system design [2], i.e., at the hardware, software and algo-
rithmic levels. For example, a software developer may use

different results than an exact algorithm. Applying approx-
imations at this level are easier; however their impact on
saving hardware resources may not be exactly as intended
due to the involvement of various compilers and optimiza-
tion steps involved. Therefore, our main focus in this paper is
the approximations done at the hardware design level. Some
of the most commonly used techniques in this regard include
(i) using reduced-precision arithmetic to reduce hardware
complexity and power consumption [3], (ii) using simpler
and smaller logic gates and components, like approximate
adders [4] and approximate multipliers [5], that compromise
accuracy by introducing a certain level of error in the given
circuit and (iii) by reducing power consumption by scaling
down the voltage level [6] supplied to the hardware system
and thus introducing errors or noise in the computation pro-
cess. s Approximate synthesis tools are extensively used in
the design and optimization of approximate circuits, as they
mainly enable designers to trade-off accuracy for reduced
power consumption, area, and delay. These tools typically
use mathematical models, based on statistical analysis or
error modeling, to estimate the level of accuracy of the syn-
thesized circuits and optimize them to meet the desired ac-
curacy constraints. Currently, several approximate synthesis
tools are available, such as ABACUS [7], SALSA[8], and
BLASYS[9]. Each of these has its own unique features and
capabilities. These tools are typically used in combination
with traditional synthesis tools to produce optimized designs
that meet the desired accuracy, power, and performance re-
quirements.
The above-mentioned approximate synthesis tools are
vulnerable to the introduction of Hardware Trojans (HTs)
[10], which are small and evasive circuits maliciously in-
troduced to alter the functionality and/or performance of a
hardware circuit in unexpected ways. An attacker could uti-
lize the approximate synthesis tool to introduce a HT into the
synthesized design and thus can potentially alter the func-
tionality of an approximate circuit or cause a shutdown ef-
fectuating resource losses in the worst case. Traditionally,
HTs are detected in digital circuits by extensive functional
testing and conducting rigorous side-channel analysis of the
synthesized designs to detect any unexpected behaviors or
anomalies. Some of these techniques are described in the
next section. However, these traditional techniques cannot
be used to detect the presence of HTs in approximate circuits
mainly because we cannot distinguish whether the differ-
ence in functionality or one of the side channel parameters

The above-mentioned security vulnerabilities of ap-
proximate circuits limit their utilization in safety and
security-critical applications [12], [13]. To effectively detect
the presence of HTs in post-synthesis approximate circuits
and thus overcome the above mentioned problem, we present
the Hardware Trojan detection using Triple modular Redun-
dancy in APproximate Synthesis (HT-TRAPS) approach in
this paper. The approach primarily utlizes Triple Modular
Redundancy (TMR) [14] along with side channel and func-
tional analysis for HT detection in approximate circuits at the
post-approximate synthesis stage at the gate level. TMR has
previously been used to detect HTs in exact post-synthesis
circuits based on path-delay measurement [15]. However,
we utilize the TMR approach in a totally different context in
HT-TRAPS. Our main objective is to facilitate the detection
of HTs in approximate circuits during the approximate syn-
thesis process, i.e., before the physical design stage, in both
ASICs or FPGA configurations. Another distinguishing fea-
ture of the proposed HT-TRAPS approach is that it returns a
single clean netlist of the required approximate circuit even
while using TMR during the process and thus it does not
introduce any additional overhead.
To illustrate the effectiveness of HT-TRAPS, we imple-
mented it using the Xilinx Vivado Design Suite, the SCOAP
tool [16], and the ABACUS [7] and BLASYS [9] syntesis
tools. HT-TRAPS was able to successfully identify the B19-
T100 (one OR gate as payload), B19-T200 (one OR gate as
payload), and B19-T500 trojan (synchrous payload) bench-
marks in an approximate absolute difference calculator (44
cells), 32-bit adder (136 cells), 16-bit multiplier (253 cells),
a classifier (581 cells), x2 (26 cells), and butterfly filter (118
cells).
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section
2 presents an overview of related work. Section 3 describes
the proposed HT-TRAPS approach and its attack and defense
mechanisms. Section 4 provides the experimental results.
Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper.
2.
Related Work
HTs [17] are a serious threat to the security of hardware-
based systems. They are often designed to remain dormant
until triggered by specific conditions, making them quite dif-
ficult to detect even during the manufacturing process. To
mitigate the risks of HTs, various techniques have been pro-
posed in the literature. Formal verification [18], [19] is a
rigorous functional analysis approach but requires a golden
netlist for comparative analysis and suffers from scalability
issues. Logical testing [20] caters for the above-mentioned
scalability issues by using a subset of all possible test vectors,
but the HTs can go undetected as the attacker can manipu-
late rare trigger conditions. Side-channel analysis [22],[24],
instead of functional comparisons, detects the HTs using
comparisons in terms of various electrical parameters, like
power and delay, during circuit operations. These methods
have been found to be more efficient than logical or behav-
ioral testing in HT detection but cannot guarantee the absence
of HTs in a circuit as well due to their dependency on test
vectors. Various novel methods, like runtime analysis [25],
and machine learning [26],[29],[28], have recently been in-
tegrated with the above-mentioned classical approaches to
improve the detection efficiency for HTs. However, to the
best of our knowledge, none of the above-mentioned tech-
niques can be directly used to detect HTs induced in approx-
imate circuits during their approximate synthesis process at
the gate level.
Recently, researchers have also made some progress in
the area of HT detection in approximate circuits. For exam-
ple, Gao et al. [30] proposed a low power obscuring security
technique where they utilized the approximation to hide the
information. The information is hidden in the Least Signifi-
cant Bits (LSB) and while the information is hidden in those
bits, the same are also used for approximation. Although
the methodology seems promising for applications, like wa-
termarking and fingerprinting, it does not entirely promise
foolproof security, since hiding information and encrypting
it using the XOR function is a well-known technique and can
easily be bypassed and decrypted.
Yellu et al. [31],[32],[33] introduced some attacks for
approximated circuits based on the type of approximation
performed at the circuit-, architecture-, and compiler-level
approximate mechanisms/algorithms. Some guidelines for
designing countermeasures were also presented, along with
a number of case studies that were included to demonstrate
how the recommended countermeasures can be put into prac-
tice. This work is quite insightful, as the authors were able
to successfully launch attacks against every approximation
that they considered. The proposed methodology is based
on traversing the finite-state machine of the given circuit and
identifying the weak links. Once identified, they separate
these from the exact modules and launch the attack on the
approximated functionality. These works clearly show that
the approximation in a circuit is one of the most vulnerable
links.
Similarly, Dou et al. [34] provide a classification of HTs
into Function-destructive Trojans and Information-leaking
Trojans, and their implantation into approximate circuits at
the gate level.
The authors analyze the security vulnera-
bilities of approximate circuits to HT insertions using error
metrics.
They find that it is more difficult to implant a
Function-destructive Trojan in an approximate circuit com-
pared to an accurate circuit, as changing the output of the
approximate circuit may even improve its accuracy. How-
ever, the approximate circuit provides new opportunities for
Information-leaking Trojans, which can leak keys without
affecting the function of approximate circuits.
Islam [35] used controllability and observability, along
with a cost function, which identifies and singles out rarely
triggered nets, to introduce HTs randomly. These HTs are
then detected by firstly assuming that they are quite prob-
able to be in the approximated modules. Then they used
path profiling and net localization with a higher probability

of carrying a HT, due to their high cost functions, which
are computed based on side channel parameters and func-
tionality. This way, the whole netlist is ranked in terms of
maximum error and side channel characteristics. Then, by
using a set of input vectors, the author achieved 90% ac-
curacy in HT detection in approximate circuits at the gate
level. Besides the relatively less accuracy, this technique is
quite compute intensive and thus may suffer from scalability
issues while dealing with larger circuits.
While majority voting using vendor diversity is a known
defense in traditional circuits, its effectiveness diminishes in
approximate circuits due to inherent error randomness and
diversity. Dou et al [36] address this gap by analyzing the
security risks posed by multi-vendor IPs for approximate
circuits at the gate level and showing the limitations of ma-
jority voting in such scenarios.
To counter this threat, a
comparison-based technique is proposed in [36], demon-
strating high effectiveness in detecting HTs in approximate
circuits. However, their comparison-based technique is only
applicable to detect HTs that are inserted in arithmetic cir-
cuits, like adders and multipliers. Moreover, the technique
only relies on functional testing and thus is susceptible to not
detecting HTs that do not cause a major behavioral change
during their inactive stage.
Reliance on third-party synthesis frameworks that sub-
stitute library components during design exploration exposes
approximate circuits to HT insertion. Ahmed et al. [37] pro-
pose a threat model highlighting the risks of Trojan insertion
during approximate accelerator synthesis. Their framework
, called MAAS, utilizes search-based synthesis to embed
Trojans in approximate circuits during the synthesis process
at the gate level.
Experimental results show that Trojan-
infected circuits produced by MAAS have a marginally larger
area than regular approximate designs and evade detection
through conventional area and power analysis. This work
is the first to demonstrate Trojan insertion in third-party ap-
proximate synthesis flows via component substitution.
Martin et al. [38] propose an effective approach to neu-
tralize HTs using an approximate version of Triple Modular
Redundancy (TMR). The method employs a fault approxi-
mation methodology to identify circuit nodes for approxima-
tion, leveraging different sets of test vectors to evaluate fault
testability and apply various approximation strategies. The
resulting under/over-approximations are used to construct
an approximate TMR that not only mitigates HT impacts
but also reduces hardware area and increases the difficulty
of Trojan insertion for gate level circuits.
Experimental
validation using ISCAS’85 benchmarks and stealthy ad-hoc
HTs demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed TMR
scheme in neutralizing HTs and enhancing hardware secu-
rity. However, the scope of this paper is not on detecting
HTs in approximate circuits but to neutralize HTs using ap-
proximations.
To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing work
that provides a scalable and robust solution for the detection
of HTs inserted in approximate circuits during their synthesis
process. In this paper, we propose the HT-TRAPS approach
that caters for these challenges by mainly leveraging upon the
strengths of TMR, functional testing and side-channel anal-
ysis based HT detection techniques. It is important to note
that Dual or Triple Modular Redundancy (DMR or TMR),
along with functional testing and side-channel analysis in
HT detection, has been previously used. For example, DMR
has been used in a prevention technique that makes it harder
to insert a stealthy HT in a gate level netlist and helps detect-
ing it during runtime [39]. Similarly, a path-level security
mechanism using selective TMR [40] is used to neutralize
HTs, ensuring resilience by targeting equally probable output
paths while maintaining detectability through logic and side-
channel analysis in gate level circuits. Moreover, a path-level
security approach for SCADA systems [41] by selectively ap-
plying TMR to equally probable output paths, mitigating the
impact of HTs while minimizing area overhead in gate level
circuit has also been proposed. However, to the best of our
knowledge, the utlization and interoperability of redundancy
and functional and side channel techniques in HT-TRAPS
for detecting HTs, inserted through the approximate synthe-
sis process, is quite novel as outlined in the next section of
this paper.
3.
Proposed Approach
The flow of the HT-TRAPS approach is depicted in Fig. 1.
It starts by triplicating the given netlist, i.e., the design that
needs to be approximated, before passing it to the approxi-
mate synthesis tool. The synthesis tool, which is susceptible
of introducing a HT, then approximates the circuit.
This
process inherently will update the functionality of the given
circuit to meet its desired objectives of optimizing the area,
power, speed and accuracy. One of the most common ways
of meeting these goals is to replace the arithmetic units of
the given circuit with their approximate versions using the
underlying algorithms of the synthesis tool. In the case of
a trust-worthy synthesis tool, all three copies of the given
circuit will get the same modifications and we will get three
identical copies of the approximated circuits.
On the other hand, if the synthesis tool is not trustwor-
thy then it may insert one or more HTs in the given circuit
and thus in our case the HTs can be introduced in one or
more copies of the approximated version of the original cir-
cuit. Traditionally, the HTs are added at the least testable
points of the design that are in turn identified based on the
controllability and observability [16] concepts.
We then analyze this post-synthesis netlist, with the
three copies of the approximated design with HTs, based
on side channel characteristics and functional analysis. If
all copies generate the same results for both these tests then
we conclude that there is no HT inserted and thus one of
three copies is chosen for the next steps of the digital design
process. On the other hand, if the comparator detects a mis-
match, either in functionality or in one of the side channel
characteristics, the mismatched copy from the three is con-
sidered to be intruded and thus discarded and the two copies
which match are assumed to be HT free and one of them

It is important to note that we proceed with only one copy
of the design and thus even though we replicated the netlist
three times during the analysis phase but there is no over-
head introduced by the HT-TRAPS approach as the other
two copies are discarded at this step. In case, all three copies
of the design lead to different results during the comparison
then HT-TRAPS has been able to detect the presence of HTs
but it will not be able to return a clean netlist.
It is important to note that the HT-TRAP approach
works under the assumption that identical HTs are not in-
serted at the same location in different copies of the circuit
by the synthesis tool. This is quite a realistic assumption as
all the three copies of the given circuit to be approximated
are fed as a single netlist to the approximate synthesis tool
so it cannot distinguish between the three copies. Synthesis
tools usually identify the least testable points of the given
netlist and then target the most optimal one for HT insertion.
Similarly, in case of multiple HT insertions, different HTs
are inserted in the least testable points.
In HT detection, an attack model represents the poten-
tial ways in which a malicious actor could introduce a HT
into a hardware design. This includes identifying the types
of attacks that could be used to introduce a Trojan, such
as fabrication or modification of the design, and the loca-
tions in the design where a Trojan could be introduced. On
the other hand, a defense model represents the methods that
can be employed to detect and prevent the introduction of a
Trojan into a hardware design. This includes identifying the
vulnerabilities in the design that could be exploited by a mali-
cious actor to introduce a Trojan, and developing techniques
to detect the presence of Trojans, such as through the use
of side-channel analysis, hardware testing, and verification
techniques. Both attack and defense models are important in
HT detection, as they provide insight into the potential vul-
nerabilities and attack vectors in a hardware design, as well
as the techniques that can be employed to prevent and detect
the introduction of Trojans. Next, we explain the attack and
defense models of the proposed HT-TRAPS approach along
with the proposed functional and side channel analysis steps
one by one.
3.1
HT Introduction (Attack)
The effectiveness of a HT detection methodology can only
be measured if the HT inserted in the circuit is generally
undetectable by the routine verification steps at every stage
of design and synthesis of a hardware. To ensure this, we
propose inserting the HT at a location in the circuit where the
observability and controllability values are low as depicted
in Fig. 2.
Controllability [16] measures the difficulty of control-
ling the logic output of a circuit by manipulating specific
logical inputs. It is inherently dependent on the logic struc-
ture and the type of gates used within the circuit. The pro-
cess of determining controllability follows a set of predefined
rules. For small circuits, this process can be performed man-
ually by analyzing each logic cell step-by-step. However, for
larger and more complex circuits, automated tools are used
to calculate the controllability of each logic unit.
The controllability values are essential for assessing ob-
servability [16], which indicates how difficult it is to observe
an output from the primary inputs. Higher observability val-
ues imply greater difficulty in tracing internal circuit activity
through the primary inputs. Tools like the Sandia Controlla-
bility and Observability Program (SCOAP) are widely used
to compute these values for both controllability and observ-
ability.
In HT-TRAPS, we leverage these controllability and
observability values to identify the most vulnerable nets for
HT insertion. By targeting nets with low controllability and
low observability, we create the most challenging scenarios
for Trojan detection. This allows us to rigorously evaluate the
detection capability of HT-TRAPS, our proposed approach
for identifying and mitigating HTs in the post-synthesis phase
of approximate circuits. Demonstrating successful detection

in these difficult scenarios underscores the robustness of
HT-TRAPS in securing approximate circuits against stealthy

Moreover, it is crucial to keep the size of the Trojan very
small to ensure that it remains undetectable. For this pur-
pose, we propose to choose the benchmarks from TrustHub
[43] which are very small and act passively.
3.2
HT Detection (Defense)
In the proposed defense approach, as depicted in Fig. 1, an
exact netlist is introduced to a Triple Modular Redundancy
(TMR) block to triplicate it. The triplicated netlist is then
processed through an approximate synthesis tool where the
approximations are applied according to the algorithms of
the given tool and the given approximation constraints. The
HT is assumed to be inserted during this synthesis process
as well. The resulting netlist, consisting of three copies of
the approximated, is then analyzed based on functionality
and side-channel characteristics and the results for the three
netlists are compared to identify the presence of a HT. If only
one of the copies has a HT then a HT-free clean copy of the
approximated circuit is also provided.
3.2.1
Functional Analysis
The functional analysis results are obtained using the behav-
ioral simulation of the approximated copies of the netlist. If
there are any differences in the output of three netlists, then it
must be due to an unwanted HT inserted in the corresponding
copy of the circuit as, due to the identical nature of the three
copies of the circuit and the same approximation algorithms
of the synthesis tool, the approximated output of all three
circuits should be the same. On the other hand, if the results
are the same then the netlist is considered to be HT free and
any one of the three copies can be synthesized for ASIC or
configured onto an FPGA device.
3.2.2
Side Channel Analysis
Just like in the functional analysis, we also propose compar-
ing the three copies among each another based on the side
channel characteristics, i.e., the power dissipation and delay
at each node. If a copy provides different results from the
remaining two, then it is assumed to be carrying a HT given
that we are getting matching results from the remaining two
copies. If all match, then all the copies are considered to be
HT free and any one of them can be used to proceed with the
rest of the digital design process.
Now, we outline the key assumptions, along with their
rationale, that ensure the effective implementation of HT-
TRAPS. These assumptions are critical for maintaining the
integrity of HT-TRAPS and the validity of the results pre-
sented in the next section:
• Assumption 1: The synthesis tool is configured with
constraints that preserve the primary input and output
interfaces during post-synthesis transformation. This
ensures that the connectivity and signal mapping of
the primary I/Os remain unchanged, allowing the three
TMR replicas to be distinguishable based on their iden-
tical external interfaces.
• Assumption 2: The approximate synthesis tool applies
identical approximation strategies to all three instances
of the triplicated circuit. This consistency ensures that
any differences observed among the instances can be at-
tributed to hardware Trojan insertions rather than vari-
ations in approximation transformations.
• Assumption 3: It is assumed that identical hardware
Trojans are not inserted at the same location across
all three replications.
This assumption is based on
how synthesis tools typically operate when embedding
HTs. Since the three circuit copies are treated as a uni-
fied netlist, the synthesis tool applies transformations
holistically rather than distinguishing between individ-
ual copies. The insertion of HTs is influenced by the
tool’s inherent non-determinism and local optimization
heuristics, which often lead to subtle variations in how
each copy is processed. As a result, it is unlikely that
an attacker’s inserted HT would be identically placed in
all three replicas. Instead, variations in synthesis trans-
formations typically result in HTs appearing in only
one or two copies, making detection feasible. Further-
more, ensuring identical HT placement across all copies
would require an unrealistic level of control over the
synthesis tool’s internal processes, which falls outside
standard operating conditions.
It is important to note that HT-TRAPS is quite probable
of detecting the presence of HTs as it is quite unlikely that
the same HT would be inserted in all three copies of the
approximated netlist. It can provide a clean netlist as well if
only one of the approximated netlist gets a HT and the other
two are clean. Moreover, by using both functional and side
channel analysis, we further increase the chances of detecting
the HTs as one of them is quite likely to catch a mismatch
between the netlists. Another worth mentioning feature of
HT-TRAPS is that it allows us to detect the HTs prior to the
physical design step in ASICs or configuring the design on
the FPGA. Thus, the HTs inserted through the approximate
synthesis process are detected before moving to the physical
design phase. Likewise, we proceed with the design process
with a single HT clean netlist so despite the utilization of
TMR method, we do not get any hardware overhead for the
three copies in the final design.
Besides offering a promising solution for detecting HTs
in approximate circuits, HT-TRAPS has its own limitations:
• One major constraint is its inability to isolate a clean
copy when multiple HTs are inserted across the three
copies of the circuit. While the presence of Trojans can
be detected, identifying a Trojan-free instance remains
challenging.
• The approach depends on specific assumptions, such as
identical transformations by the approximate synthesis

tool and invariant primary I/O constraints. Any devia-
tions from these assumptions can impact the detection
accuracy.
• Scalability is another challenge, as HT-TRAPS requires
functional and side-channel analyses of a triplicated
circuit, necessitating resources capable of handling a
circuit three times larger than the original design and
comparing the outputs of all three copies.
Under the given assumptions, HT-TRAPS reports ab-
sence of HTs only when the results of functional and side
channel analyses are the same for all the three copies. This
can happen in the following two scenarios:
• There is no HT inserted by the approximate synthesis
tool, i.e., a True Negative.
• There are multiple identical HTs added at the same
locations of all three netlistsand thusHT-TRAPScannot
distinguish between the approximation update and the
trojan insertion. This is a False Negative.
We can safely mention that the possibility of False Neg-
atives is a function of redundancy and number of inserted
HTs. For example, in case of triplicating the circuit, we can
have no False Negatives as long as the inserted HTs is less
than 3. In general terms, we will not have any False Negative
if we replicate the circuit 𝑛times to safeguard against 𝑛−1
HTs.
On the other hand, increasing the redundancy increases
the circuit size and thus negatively impacts the scalability of
the approach as mentioned above. We propose to triplicate
the given circuit in HT-TRAPS as we need at least three
copies to be able to return a clean copy of the netlist.
4.
Experimental Results
We implement HT-TRAPS using BLASYS and ABACUS as
our synthesis tools, SCOAP for controllability and observ-
ability analysis and Xilinx Vivado Design Suite for func-
tional and side channel analysis. By using Xilinx Vivado
Design Suite, we are targeting the FPGA implementations,
but it is important to note that HT-TRAPS is generic and is
equally applicable to ASIC designs as well. BLASYS and
ABACUS are open source approximate synthesis tools that
accept Verilog netlists. The approximated netlist is intro-
duced to the SCOAP analysis tool for obtaining the control-
lability and observability values for each net and thus decide
where to insert the HT.
For illustration, we first apply HT-TRAPS on an Ab-
solute difference (abs-diff) calculator from the Benchmarks
for Approximate Circuit Synthesis (BACS) [42], which is
used to determine the approximated difference between two
inputs and is composed of 184 gates and 225 nets.
The
design is first triplicated and then approximated using the
Mean Absolute Error (MAE) metric. The approximate de-
sign is generated using the Circuit Carving technique. The
B19-T100 benchmark, given in Fig. 3, from Trust Hub [43]
is then inserted in the design. The location of the B19-T100
is selected based on the controllability and observability val-
ues obtained through the SCOAP tool so that it not easy to
detect, i.e., at the least testable point.

5.
Conclusions
Approximate computing allows compromising the numerical
accuracy of computer arithmetic to obtain power, speed and
area gains. It is being widely advocated for error-tolerant
applications these days. However, approximate circuits are
highly susceptible to HTs during the approximate synthesis
process. These HTs are also very challenging to detect as
differentiating them from an approximation update is almost
impossible in the post-synthesis stage.
In this paper, we
propose to solve the above-mentioned challenge by using
TMR along with functional and side channel analysis in the
proposed HT-TRAPS approach. The effectiveness of HT-
TRAPS is illustrated using 6 benchmarks. Each benchmark
was inserted with 3 Trojan benchmarks and the success rate
for HT identification is found to be 100%. In future, we
plan to integrate the replay method [44] in our approach and
evaluate its efficacy compared to TMR.
